 No bites, no delays: TSA safely resolves slithery discovery at Ontario International 
 Friday, November 13, 2026 
 TSA officers at California’s Ontario International Airport (ONT) encountered a potentially scary discovery while screening a checked bag. What initially appeared to be rope was actually two live snakes concealed inside a pillowcase.
 While conducting a routine inspection of the bag, TSA Officer Benjamin Andrade-Carillo noticed the pillowcase and began examining it.
 “When I realized the item in my hand was alive, I told myself, ‘I need to escalate this immediately,’” Andrade-Carillo recalled. 
 He promptly notified Supervisory TSA Officer Suggey Flores.
 After arriving at the checked baggage screening area, Flores assessed the situation and carefully examined the bag.
 “I felt it tense up and start moving,” Flores said. “I have held snakes before, so I wasn’t too spooked. I was more impressed, because it’s not something you see every day.”
 TSA officers discovered two live snakes in this green pillowcase while searching through a passenger’s checked bag. (TSA ONT photo) 
 Flores notified ONT TSA Manager Francisco “Frank” Calderon, airport police and the passenger’s airline. Calderon saw the bag move and confirmed live snakes were inside, one of which was a rattlesnake. 
 “TSA officers should not be handling live snakes for safety reasons,” Calderon said. “Our priority was ensuring the safety of our officers and everyone in the area while making the proper notifications and coordinating a safe resolution.”
 Screening was briefly paused in the immediate area, primarily due to safety concerns. 
 “Safety was a concern because we didn’t know what kind of snakes they were,” Flores said. “They could have been venomous.”
 Airport police took possession of the bag and brought it to the airline ticketing area, where the passenger removed the snakes and gave them to a non-traveling family member who took custody of the animals.
 After the snakes were removed, TSA rescreened the checked bag and cleared it for travel. The airline allowed the passenger to fly without the snakes. The incident did not disrupt overall screening operations at ONT.
 According to the Los Angeles TSA Coordination Center, the passenger said the snakes were pets and he had traveled with them previously on another airline. TSA advises travelers to contact their airline before arriving at the airport to understand the carrier’s requirements for traveling with pets, including reptiles.
 From left, TSA Officer Benjamin Andrade-Carillo, Supervisory TSA Officer Suggey Flores and ONT TSA Manager Francisco “Frank” Calderon (TSA ONT photo) 
 “In my two years of service, I had not found anything like this,” Andrade-Carillo said. “In San Diego, I experienced a gentleman trying to bring live lobsters as a carry-on.”
 Andrade-Carillo encouraged travelers to be mindful of what they pack.
 “We ask the traveling public to be mindful of what they bring in their bags,” he said, “because if we don’t know what it is, we will find out.”
 Calderon praised the officers’ response.
 “I am very happy with the way our team handled the situation, stopped screening when they needed to and made the proper notifications,” Calderon said. “No injuries or bites were reported, thank goodness.”
 Jason Pantages, TSA’s federal security director for Los Angeles International and surrounding airports, also recognized the ONT team for its response.
 “Our officers are trained to respond calmly and professionally to unexpected situations while keeping safety at the forefront,” said Pantages. “This incident demonstrates the sound judgment and teamwork of the ONT TSA workforce as well as the importance of travelers checking with their airline before bringing animals, including reptiles, to the airport.”
 By Don Wagner. TSA Strategic Communications & Public Affairs
